cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), mostly plantation leaf and sorted fragments
processing: Raw pu-erh maocha, usually lower grades and broken leaf, is steamed and machine-pressed into 3–5 g nest-shaped tuo and wrapped individually in foil or paper; sheng versions are the minority next to shu mini tuo.
harvest_season: Pressed from any season's maocha, often summer and autumn leaf, and sold without much reference to harvest.
appearance_dry: A hard, smooth little nest with a dimple on the bottom, dark green with small bits of bud and visible fragments.
appearance_liquor: Yellow to orange-gold, often cloudy in the first steep from fine particles.
appearance_wet: Small broken leaves and fragments that take a while to loosen from the dense core.
taste_profile: Straightforward and strong: a sharp bitterness, grassy and woody notes, a quick thin sweetness and a short finish; built for a mug, not a tasting.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water, the second rinse for 20–30 seconds, to break the compression. One tuo per 120–150 ml; the first proper steep needs 30–40 seconds and the pieces open fully by the third. Fine for grandpa-style in a big mug.

vintage_note: Sold by weight or by count in bags, tins and gift boxes, generally with a production year on the packaging and rarely with a harvest season or origin; most are pressed from recent plantation leaf and sold within a year or two. They age slowly because of the hard compression and are not bought to cellar, though 5–10-year-old factory mini tuo from the Dali and Kunming plants do turn up and can be pleasant. Treat the year as a freshness date rather than a vintage, and treat anything described as gushu in this format with disbelief.
description:
Mini tuo are single-serving nests of pu-erh, roughly 3–5 g each, pressed by machine and wrapped one by one, and the sheng version is the raw-tea counterpart of the ripe mini tuo that fill supermarket gift boxes. They are the cheapest and most convenient form of pu-erh and, honestly, usually the roughest.

The material is typically lower-grade maocha and sorted fragments from plantation gardens, steamed and pressed hard into a dimpled nest so that a single piece makes a mug or a small pot. The compression is severe, so the tea opens slowly, releases a lot of fine particles and changes very little in storage.

In the cup, a sheng mini tuo is strong and direct: bitter, grassy, woody, with a thin quick sweetness and a short finish; the first steep is often cloudy. It improves a lot with a double rinse and a long first infusion, and it is better in a big mug with hot water topped up than in a careful gaiwan session. A few years of age round it off noticeably.

They are sold by count and weight, often with a production year and seldom with an origin, in tins and boxes aimed at gifts and offices. The thing to know is simply what they are: everyday tea at everyday prices, not a compact gushu. The better ones come from the established Dali and Kunming factories; the worst are dust pressed with scented flavourings, which you can smell through the wrapper.

If you like the single-serve idea but want to taste real material, dragon balls are the same convenience with far better leaf.
history:
The mini tuo is a format, not a tea from one place. It takes the dome-with-a-dimple shape of the standard 100 g tuocha and shrinks it to a nugget of 3 to 5 g, enough for one pot or cup. Chinese calls it xiao tuocha, simply small tuo.

Little is documented about who first pressed raw pu-erh this way or when. It is best understood as a convenience format of modern production, with no regional story of its own.
